extracted.intended_audience: electric cooperative leaders, policymakers, and co-op advocacy staff
extracted.subtask_short: co-op advocacy on permitting and reliability
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reporting about federal policy, funding, permitting, and advocacy priorities electric cooperatives should pursue to preserve reliable, affordable power during the energy transition. Includes recommended messaging and specific programmatic/legislative fixes to support co-ops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability as the top policy priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability is 'job one' for electric co-ops; policymakers should prioritize grid reliability amid the energy transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice reliability while pursuing decarbonization; co-ops and policymakers should ensure systems remain 'dispatchable, reliable and affordable.' Emphasize always-available generation (nuclear, hydropower, fossil) to back up intermittent resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting reform to speed and provide certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal permitting processes must be streamlined so co-ops can build transmission, generation and distribution capacity in a timely way (support for SPEED Act, PERMIT Act, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should expedite NEPA reviews and Clean Water Act permitting, strip reviews down to what statutes require, coordinate agencies (CEQ role), and provide lasting statutory fixes so policy doesn't 'boomerang' with each administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit litigation timelines for permitting challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting-related litigation should have reasonable time limits so it does not delay crucial infrastructure projects for years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for statutory or procedural limits on how long challengers can sue or otherwise delay permitting decisions to avoid multi-year project hold-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: RUS loan program: increase funding and lending flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the Rural Utilities Service (RUS) Electric Loan Program funding levels and allow the agency to lend up to a higher percentage above statutory loan authority (NRECA supports up to 50% over threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that RUS lending should be 'driven by the needs of the borrower rather than limiting the types of projects eligible' and that program flexibility is needed to support distribution, transmission, environmental upgrades, or new generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify RUS funding increases on repayment and fiscal benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: RUS electric loans are repaid with interest and can reduce the federal deficit (example: fiscal year 2024 netted $179 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repayment/fiscal return arguments when asking appropriators to increase funding—emphasize borrower repayment history and deficit reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE program funding and faster award processes
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE initiatives (GRIP, SPARK, etc.) and other grant programs should fund co-op projects and speed up the award and implementation timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight delays (awards taking two to three years) and press DOE to accelerate application review and award timelines; point to specific programs (GRIP, SPARK) and funding opportunities to support reconductoring, advanced transmission technologies, and resource adequacy studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand and use reconductoring and transmission upgrades (SPARK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconductor existing lines (replace with higher-capacity conductors) is a cost-effective way to increase capacity and improve reliability and affordability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote reconductoring as using current infrastructure to 'get more electrons onto the grid' and include reconductoring projects as eligible for federal demonstration/funding opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army Corps Nationwide Permit expansion for minimal-impact utility activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand the use of Nationwide Permits under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act to authorize minimal-impact activities like construction and maintenance of utility power lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide co-op input on proposed changes (comments due May 15 in the cited instance); argue expansion reduces permitting barriers and provides faster authorizations for routine utility work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide granular mapping for Clean Water Act jurisdictional certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Create detailed maps to identify water bodies subject to federal regulation so co-ops and utilities have greater certainty about permitting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that mapping reduces project delays and compliance uncertainty and should be part of permit-streamlining efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedite approvals and financing for hydropower upgrades
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Corps is evaluating ways to expand hydropower production and attract outside financing to accelerate approvals for hydropower facility upgrades and electrifying dams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support measures that speed approvals and promote financing mechanisms to unlock hydropower's affordable, reliable generation potential for co-ops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wildfire mitigation permitting and liability reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Expedite permitting and approvals for wildfire mitigation projects on federal lands and reduce or eliminate strict liability rules that hold co-ops accountable for fires they did not cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for consistent, expedited utility permitting across national forests (use Midstate Electric example) and for statutory or administrative liability reforms to lower risk and enable timely vegetation management, undergrounding, pole replacement, and ROW expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct-pay incentives and federal incentives to help co-ops invest in renewables
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct-pay incentives (and other federal incentives) can help co-ops afford investments in renewable energy projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push for eligibility and access to incentives for co-ops (parity in incentives) and highlight how direct-pay can unlock investments while protecting member rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy principle: follow up and persistent engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stay in regular contact with agencies and lawmakers on policy priorities—'Follow up. That is the biggest thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After meetings or submissions, continue engaging with staff, provide requested information, and maintain visibility on your issues to keep them moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy messaging: ground arguments in concrete, local examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective advocacy is 'grounded in reality'—tell lawmakers specific stories: 'Here’s my project. Here’s the delay. Here’s what it’s costing us. Here’s what would fix it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use project-specific details and local impacts rather than only statistics; provide cost estimates, timelines, and suggested fixes to persuade policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent, nonpartisan messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-ops should deliver a consistent message about the need for reliable, affordable power 'no matter which political party is in control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame issues as transcending party lines; emphasize community service and practical impacts to maintain bipartisan support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask large electricity users (e.g., data centers) to pay incremental infrastructure costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold big tech/data centers responsible for paying for extra power and infrastructure they require so existing customers’ rates remain stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose cost-allocation mechanisms or contractual requirements requiring large new loads to fund necessary distribution/transmission upgrades to avoid rate pressure on existing members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community outreach to build project support
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage members and communities through outreach events to gather input and answer questions, which helps advance large projects (KIUC's Kaawanui Solar example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document community benefits (cost savings, jobs, emissions avoided), host public meetings, and incorporate feedback to reduce opposition and inform project design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standard for seeking stays: demonstrate irreparable harm and risk to public
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing amicus briefs or seeking stays of injunctions, emphasize irreparable harm to consumers (higher costs, reduced grid stability, blackout risk) and that lower courts exceeded authority under APA/other statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame harms quantitatively where possible (e.g., projected MW losses, % rate increases) and tie arguments to public safety, national security, and statutory limits on judicial remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate for broad eligibility of federal lending and grant programs
rubrics_metrics.description: RUS and similar programs should support a wide range of projects (distribution, transmission, environmental upgrades, new generation) rather than narrowly limiting eligible project types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request statutory/regulatory flexibility in program guidance and funding notices so borrowers can meet diverse local needs as demand and technology change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory certainty is required for long-term investment decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilities need stable, statutory policy frameworks (not shifting administrative policy) to justify capital-intensive investments with multi-decade asset lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push for legislative fixes that lock in permitting/process reforms and provide predictable rules so co-ops will commit to long-term projects.
